title: Backbench and Junior Office
note: The House, the ward and the first rungs of office: MP (rank 8), Parliamentary Secretary and Senior Parliamentary Secretary (9-10), with one card for office holders (11-16). The four House cards pick a backbench or an office-holder version by rank (the role part). Ward cards stop at 10 on purpose: the pool at 11-14 is where The Reshuffle raises the ceiling, and every card there dilutes it. Backbench cards trade Reputation against Standing with the Whip; junior office cards trade Integrity against Standing with the Minister. Parts and the cast make one card many scenes: the bill and the Whip's text, the ministry a promise belongs to, the facility residents petition against. The two seat cards are exclusive: The Next Ward needs seat_grc, The Other Candidate seat_smc.

events.title: The Whip's Text

options.a: Vote with the party. Send your view to the party's committee on the bill.
options.aOut: You vote with the party and email your view to the committee's chairman, who replies with a thumbs-up. The bill passes. Your view is filed with the thumbs-up.
options.b: Speak against {bill.short}. Then vote for the bill.
options.bOut: Your eleven minutes against {bill.short} go into Hansard. So does your vote for the bill, an hour later. A resident writes to ask which one you meant. You write back: both.

options.a: Vote with the party. Keep your view to yourself.
options.aOut: You vote with the party and the bill passes. Your view stays in a note on your phone, under a heading you do not open again.
options.b: Put your view to the bill's Minister. Then vote for it.
options.bOut: The bill's Minister hears you out over kopi and accepts one change to {bill.short}: a comma. Your vote goes in with everyone else's. The comma goes into the Act.

msg.text: "Pls be in the Chamber by 3pm tmr. Thx."
"2nd Reading tmr. Want a slot to speak? Pls advise."

bill.text: data-sharing between nine agencies, without asking residents
new powers for a government agency, with appeals to its own Minister
higher fines for parking offences in public housing car parks

events.body: At 10:52pm the Whip texts: {msg} Tomorrow's bill brings in {bill}. You think it is wrong; the party supports it. Members vote the party line unless the Whip lifts the whip, and crossing the Whip costs you standing.

choices.text: Ask the Whip to lift the whip.
choices.outcome: The Whip replies at 7am: "Not this one." You vote with the party. The Whip now keeps a short list of the bills you would like to be this one.

options.body: You have won the ballot for tonight's adjournment motion: twenty minutes, at the end of a long sitting, to raise {topic}, and a minister must reply. Backbenchers rarely get to pick the subject. {house}
options.a: Speak for the full twenty minutes.
options.aOut: Twenty minutes on {topic.short}, at 9:40pm. The reply takes ten. Then Parliament does now adjourn, exactly as your motion proposed, and everyone goes home.
options.b: Cut it to five. Let the House go home.
options.bOut: Five minutes, and the House is grateful in the lift. The reply, written for twenty minutes of argument, is read out in full, at the usual pace.
options.c: Send the ministry your speech the day before.
options.cOut: The reply answers every point you make, in order, including the one you cut at 9:38pm. You have never been so thoroughly answered, or so little reported.

options.body: {mp} has won the ballot for tonight's adjournment motion, a twenty-minute speech on something your ministry handles. The reply falls to you: ten minutes, at about ten o'clock, answering a colleague from your own party in public. {draft}
options.a: Concede the point {mp} is right about.
options.aOut: You concede it in your second minute and spend the other eight on what will change. {mp} thanks you across the floor. Your officials thank you less.
options.b: Read the draft, at a steady pace.
options.bOut: The reply is read in full. {mp} listens with the face of a colleague, then posts the speech online with your reply beneath it, unedited.
options.c: Call {mp} beforehand, and agree the exchange.
options.cOut: The exchange goes as agreed, which nobody watching can tell. {mp} thanks you in the lift. The newspaper calls the debate "cordial" and gives it two paragraphs.

topic.text: the bus service your ward lost in the last route review
caregivers who earn slightly too much for every scheme
lifts that are upgraded on schedule and break down off it

house.text: {journalist}, the only reporter left in the press gallery, has brought a sandwich.
By then the Chamber will hold eleven Members and the Clerks.
Most Members still there are waiting for the item after yours: going home.

draft.text: Your officials' draft reply concedes nothing, beautifully.
The draft reply runs to twelve minutes. You have ten.
Your officials finished the draft reply before the speech it answers was written.

options.body: At the Committee of Supply, the yearly debate on each ministry's budget, you want a few minutes to speak. To get them, you have filed a motion to cut {head}'s budget by $100, as Parliament's rules allow. Nobody expects the cut to pass. Your ward wants {head.ward}. You also have a harder question.
options.a: Ask for what your ward wants.
options.aOut: The Minister promises, by name, to study {head.ward}. In your ward, that counts as delivery. You ask leave to withdraw your amendment. Leave is granted.
options.bOut: The Minister answers carefully, and for longer than planned. You ask leave to withdraw your $100. It is granted, a little more slowly than the others.
options.c: Ask the question your party committee agreed on, word for word.
options.cOut: Four Members ask it in the same words. The Minister answers it once, warmly, and all four ask leave to withdraw their $100. The budget is unchanged by $400.

options.body: At the Committee of Supply, the yearly debate on each ministry's budget, Members have filed eleven token cuts of $100 to your ministry's budget, the usual way to get time to speak, and four of the replies are yours. One Member wants something for a ward. Another has asked a harder question.
options.a: Promise the Member a study, naming the ward.
options.aOut: You promise, naming the ward, to study it. Its residents count that as delivery. Your officials count it as a new workstream, with a deadline you have just set.
options.b: Answer the harder cut properly, past your time.
options.bOut: You run four minutes over on the harder cut. The Member asks leave to withdraw the $100, and thanks you in a tone that sounds, unusually, sincere.
options.c: Read the replies your officials drafted.
options.cOut: The replies are accurate, and written for the questions the ministry expected. All four Members ask leave to withdraw their $100 anyway. That is what the $100 is for.

head.ward: a sheltered walkway to the train station
a polyclinic nearer than the next town's

lifts for the three blocks the upgrading missed

options.body: Your GPC, the party's committee of backbench MPs who shadow one ministry, is briefed, behind closed doors, on a scheme you worked on in the service. The briefer is {peer}, {peer.aTitle} now, who started in the service the same week as you. Slide nine leaves out the scheme's weakest number, just as you would have. Asking about it would put {peer} on the spot in front of MPs.
options.a: Ask about what slide nine leaves out.
options.aOut: {peer} answers it fully, with a figure you recognise. Afterwards {peer} sends one word: "Thanks." Slide nine, you realise, was left that way for somebody to ask.
options.bOut: The GPC thanks {peer}, and {peer} thanks the GPC. The scheme goes ahead as briefed, weak number and all. GPCs publish no minutes, so the thanks are the only record.
options.c: Ask {peer} about it afterwards, over kopi.
options.cOut: {peer} comes for kopi, talks about old colleagues for forty minutes, and says of the scheme only: "It's in the briefing." It was, on page forty of the annex.

options.body: As an office holder you must brief a GPC, the party's committee of backbench MPs who shadow your ministry, behind closed doors, on one of its schemes. The slides are by {peer}, {peer.aTitle} now, who started in the service the same week as you. Slide nine leaves out the scheme's weakest number. The MPs will not know unless you tell them.
options.a: Tell them what slide nine leaves out.
options.aOut: In a closed room, out loud, you name what is missing, and the GPC asks better questions for an hour. Afterwards {peer} sends one word: "Thanks." The slide had been left that way for you.
options.bOut: The GPC thanks you, and you thank the GPC. The scheme goes ahead as briefed, weak number and all. GPCs publish no minutes, so the thanks are the only record.
options.cOut: {peer} presents slide nine flawlessly and takes the hard question for you. Afterwards {peer} asks, lightly, whether you will be needing anyone for slide ten.

events.title: The Letter Writer

writer.text: Mr Ang, twenty-six years at the folding table
Darren, a law student who types very fast

trick.text: Every resident in {writer.short}'s letters earns slightly less than on the forms.
Every family in {writer.short}'s letters has an elderly parent who has just had a fall.
{Writer.short}'s letters cite a paragraph of the policy that does not exist, with great confidence.

events.body: At your weekly Meet-the-People Session, volunteers write residents' appeals to agencies. One agency's reply notes, politely, a discrepancy that leads to your best letter writer, {writer}. {trick} The letters work better than anyone else's, and every one goes out on your letterhead.

choices.text: Stop it. Send every agency a correction.
choices.outcome: Corrections go to eleven agencies under your name. Four cases are reconsidered and three refused. {Writer.short} stays on, and now writes what the forms say, more slowly.

choices.text: Leave it. The cases are real, if not the details.
choices.outcome: The letters keep working. In the agency that noticed, someone opens a file of discrepancies, and every page of it is on your letterhead.

choices.text: Read and sign every letter yourself from now on.
choices.outcome: Your Tuesdays now end at one in the morning. The letters are accurate, and slightly less persuasive. {Writer.short} brings you kopi at eleven, and you understand it to be a review.

events.title: Not at This Block

site.text: an eldercare centre at the void deck, the open ground floor, of Blk 118
site.later: Two years after it opens, the woman who started the petition drops her mother there on weekdays.

site.text: a nursing home on the field beside the playground
site.later: Three years after it opens, the block's choir sings there on Sundays. Two of the altos signed the petition.

site.text: a halfway house in the old school building
site.later: Five years on, two of its former residents work at the coffee shop that started the petition. Nobody brings it up.

objection.text: A petition against it has 412 signatures and a Facebook group.
You have had 61 emails about it, all with the same subject line.
{grassroots} reports that the coffee shop is against it, and so is {grassroots.their} own block.

events.body: A ministry has picked a site in your ward for {site}. {objection} The agency running it wants you, as the ward's MP, beside it at Saturday's dialogue with residents, and the residents who vote for you will see where you stand.

choices.text: Stand beside the agency. Say it is needed.
choices.outcome: On Saturday you say so, and are heckled, politely, for forty minutes. {site.later}

choices.text: Ask the ministry to look at other sites.
choices.outcome: The ministry finds a site two towns away. That ward has a petition too, with more signatures, and its MP rings you to ask how you did it.

choices.text: Back it, if residents get something for the space.
choices.outcome: {Site.short} shrinks by a fifth, the residents get a fitness corner, and the agency gets its site a year late. Everyone describes this as a win, separately.

events.title: The Arrears

who.text: a retired cleaner at Blk 52 who pays $20 whenever she can
a hawker who lost three months' takings when the market was renovated
a widower who comes to your Tuesday session every month to apologise for it

events.body: At the meeting of your Town Council, which runs the estates in your ward, the managing agent proposes taking households more than six months behind on their S&CC, the monthly charges for the estate's upkeep, to court. Forty are on the list, and it needs the council's approval. One of them is {who}.

choices.text: Approve it. The rules apply to everyone.
choices.outcome: Thirty-one households pay within a month of the letters. Nine go to court, among them {who.short}, who brings the court's letter to your next Tuesday session.

choices.text: Take one name off the list, quietly.
choices.outcome: Thirty-nine households get the letter. {Who.short} does not, and never learns why. At the next meeting the managing agent's list has a footnote, and the footnote is you.

choices.text: Change it for everyone: payment plans before courts.
choices.outcome: Nobody goes to court. Arrears rise for a quarter, then fall below where they began. The agent presents the chart to three Town Councils as a warning, and to a fourth as advice.

events.title: The Next Ward

reason.text: you once wrote a letter there that worked

events.body: Your GRC is split into wards, one for each MP on the team. Blk 438 is in {mp}'s ward, but its residents come to your Meet-the-People Session, your weekly evening for residents' problems, because {reason}. {mp} has mentioned this at the team's breakfast, as a joke, twice. It sounds less like a joke the second time.

choices.text: Keep seeing them. Residents choose.
choices.outcome: Blk 438 keeps coming. {mp} stops mentioning it at breakfast. That is worse. In the team's newsletter photograph you stand at one end and {mp} at the other.

choices.text: Send them to {mp}, with a note on every case.
choices.outcome: {mp} sees every one of them, properly, and thanks you at breakfast without a joke. By March {mp}'s session also ends later. Two residents still come to yours.

choices.text: Propose a joint session for the block.
choices.outcome: Every fourth Tuesday, Blk 438 gets both of you at one table. Residents explain each case twice, once to each MP, and leave sure it will be done twice as fast.

events.title: The Other Candidate

where.text: Saturday mornings at the train station exit
every weekend in the hawker centre's breakfast queue

events.body: The opposition candidate you beat at the last election has not stopped campaigning in your ward: {where}, in a party T-shirt, shaking hands you shook first. If residents warm to them, your single seat is at risk next time. The chairman of your party branch, the party's volunteers in your ward, would like you out there too, in your own T-shirt.

choices.text: Match them, every weekend.
choices.outcome: For a year, two T-shirts work the same stalls an hour apart. Residents compare you, in detail, out loud. Your papers for the House are read on Sunday nights.

choices.text: Leave them to it. Do the work instead.
choices.outcome: Your weekends go to cases and papers. The other candidate is photographed with more residents than you are, and your branch chairman cuts the photographs out for you.

choices.text: Invite them for kopi.
choices.outcome: They accept. You talk about the lifts for an hour and agree on most of it. The photograph is online by noon, and the Whip asks, kindly, whose idea it was.

events.title: The Date

promise.text: the lifts at Blk 210 will be upgraded by Chinese New Year
promise.made: The lifts open on the eve of Chinese New Year. On the first day of the New Year one of them stops between floors, with two families and a mandarin orange plant inside.

promise.text: a new bus service will start in March
promise.made: The service starts in March with buses borrowed from three other routes. Those three now come every twenty minutes, and their passengers write to you.

promise.text: the new polyclinic will open by December
promise.made: The polyclinic opens in the last week of December with a pharmacy, a waiting area and two doctors. The other ten arrive in June, as your officials said.

promise.text: the school's new hall will be ready for next year's Primary One
promise.made: The hall is ready in January and the air-conditioning in April. Primary One learns the school song in record time, in a very warm hall.

requires.ministry: Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment

promise.text: the drain works on the main road will be done before the monsoon
promise.made: The drain is finished in November, and works. The contractor's overtime appears in next year's budget, under drains.

promise.text: the new neighbourhood police post will open by National Day
promise.made: The post opens on 8 August, staffed and freshly painted. The paint is still wet on National Day. The officers mention this to everyone who leans on it.

promise.text: the careers centre at the community club will open next month
promise.made: It opens next month with two career coaches, a printer and no internet. The internet arrives in month five, along with most of the jobseekers.

requires.ministry: Ministry of Social and Family Development

promise.text: the new family service centre will open next month
promise.real: the autumn, once the lease is signed
promise.made: It opens next month in a room borrowed from the community club, between a karaoke class and a line-dancing one. The caseworkers learn to time their calls.

requires.ministry: Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry

promise.text: the grant for neighbourhood shops will open next month
promise.made: The grant opens next month, with a form that asks for information it will only need next year. Eleven shops apply. Two of them understand the form.

promise.text: the household payouts will arrive before the school holidays
promise.made: The payouts arrive a week before the holidays. The hotline takes forty thousand calls that week, most of them asking what the money is for.

events.body: On a visit with your Minister, the Minister tells a crowd of residents that {promise}. Your officials, standing behind you, have told you it will really be {promise.real}. The cameras are still on, and the residents will hold the ministry to the date they just heard.

choices.text: Correct the date now, beside the Minister.
choices.outcome: You say, gently, that it will be {promise.real}. The Minister says, "Better to under-promise," without missing a beat. The clip is of the Minister. The car ride back is quiet.

choices.text: Tell the Minister in the car.
choices.outcome: The Minister thanks you, and gives the right date at the next visit, crediting your officials. The residents at the first visit remember the first date, and keep asking after it.

choices.text: Ask your officials to make the date.
choices.outcome: {promise.made}

events.title: The Stand-In

event.text: a trade association's fiftieth anniversary dinner

story.short: in a kampong with one well
story.guest: Afterwards a guest says, delighted, that he grew up in the same kampong, and asks which house.

story.text: selling kueh at a market at six every morning
story.guest: Afterwards a guest asks which market, because her family sold kueh there too, and would remember you.

story.text: a grandmother's provision shop and its abacus
story.guest: Afterwards a guest asks whether the shop is still there. Gone, you say. It is true of some shop, somewhere.

events.body: Your Minister is overseas, so tonight's speech at {event} is yours. It was written for the Minister, and nobody has changed it: paragraph three is the Minister's own childhood, in the first person, {story}. You are on in ten minutes.

choices.text: Read it as written.
choices.outcome: You spend two minutes growing up {story.short}, and it lands. {story.guest}

choices.text: Cut paragraph three, and read the rest.
choices.outcome: The speech runs four minutes short and has no middle. Dinner is served early, and the evening is remembered, warmly, for the dinner.

choices.text: Tell your own story instead.
choices.outcome: Your own childhood, unrehearsed, is less tidy than the Minister's. It gets the only real laugh of the night. The Minister's office asks for a copy, for the files.

events.title: The Other Side of the Table
events.body: The party asks you to sit on the panel at a tea, its first, informal look at a possible election candidate. The candidate is {peer}, {peer.aTitle} now, who started in the service the same week as you and does not know you will be there. The file is thin and very good. Knowing a candidate is meant to be declared.

choices.text: Say that you know {peer}, and step aside.
choices.outcome: The tea goes ahead without you, and you hear nothing about it, correctly. The party does not field {peer}, who stays in the service and never mentions the tea, which you take as good manners.

choices.text: Say that you know {peer}, and sit anyway.
choices.outcome: The panel lets you stay. You ask {peer} about the folder, gently, in the voice that once asked you. {peer} answers it better than you did, and the party still decides not to field {peer}.

choices.text: Sit, and say nothing about knowing {peer}.
choices.outcome: Nobody asks, and you are fair, mostly. {peer} is not fielded, and stays in the service. A year later, at a wedding, {peer} thanks you for the panel, in front of two people who were also on it.
